claim: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVs) in the dentate gyrus provide activity-dependent regulation of adult neurogenesis.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVs) in the dentate gyrus provide activity-dependent regulation of adult neurogenesis as well as maintain inhibitory control of mature neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this relationship.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons maintain inhibitory control of mature neurons.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVs) in the dentate gyrus provide activity-dependent regulation of adult neurogenesis as well as maintain inhibitory control of mature neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: In mature neurons, PVs evoke GABAA postsynaptic currents (GPSCs) with fast rise and decay phases.
source: In mature neurons, PVs evoke GABAA postsynaptic currents (GPSCs) with fast rise and decay phases that allow precise control of spike timing, yet synaptic currents with fast kinetics do not appear in adult-born neurons until several weeks after cell birth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is also demonstrated in the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fast GPSCs from PVs allow precise control of spike timing in mature neurons.
source: In mature neurons, PVs evoke GABAA postsynaptic currents (GPSCs) with fast rise and decay phases that allow precise control of spike timing, yet synaptic currents with fast kinetics do not appear in adult-born neurons until several weeks after cell birth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the functional role of fast GPSCs.

claim: Synaptic currents with fast kinetics do not appear in adult-born neurons until several weeks after cell birth.
source: In mature neurons, PVs evoke GABAA postsynaptic currents (GPSCs) with fast rise and decay phases that allow precise control of spike timing, yet synaptic currents with fast kinetics do not appear in adult-born neurons until several weeks after cell birth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is consistent with the experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: PV-evoked currents in mature neurons exhibit fast rise and decay phases.
source: Whereas PV-evoked currents in mature neurons exhibit hallmark fast rise and decay phases, newborn neurons display slow GPSCs with characteristics of spillover signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and throughout the manuscript.

claim: Newborn neurons display slow GPSCs with characteristics of spillover signaling in response to PV activation.
source: Whereas PV-evoked currents in mature neurons exhibit hallmark fast rise and decay phases, newborn neurons display slow GPSCs with characteristics of spillover signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1, 3, and throughout the manuscript.

claim: Slow spillover currents can be unmasked in mature neurons in the absence of fast GPSCs.
source: We also unmasked slow spillover currents in mature neurons in the absence of fast GPSCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: PVs mediate slow spillover signaling in addition to conventional fast synaptic signaling.
source: Our results suggest that PVs mediate slow spillover signaling in addition to conventional fast synaptic signaling, and that spillover transmission mediates activity-dependent regulation of early events in adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Spillover transmission mediates activity-dependent regulation of early events in adult neurogenesis.
source: Our results suggest that PVs mediate slow spillover signaling in addition to conventional fast synaptic signaling, and that spillover transmission mediates activity-dependent regulation of early events in adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings combined with prior knowledge about PV regulation of neurogenesis.

claim: The dentate gyrus contains neural stem cells that continually generate new glutamatergic neurons (granule cells) throughout life.
source: The dentate gyrus contains neural stem cells that continually generate new glutamatergic neurons, the granule cells (GCs), throughout life.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus.

claim: Adult neurogenesis proceeds in a step-wise manner with activated stem cells producing rapidly dividing progenitor cells.
source: Adult neurogenesis proceeds in a step-wise manner, with activated stem cells producing rapidly dividing progenitor cells that exit cell cycle and differentiate into newborn GCs or undergo programmed cell death, followed by a prolonged period of synaptic integration (Toni and Schinder, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Toni and Schinder, 2015).

claim: Progenitor cells exit cell cycle and differentiate into newborn GCs or undergo programmed cell death.
source: Adult neurogenesis proceeds in a step-wise manner, with activated stem cells producing rapidly dividing progenitor cells that exit cell cycle and differentiate into newborn GCs or undergo programmed cell death, followed by a prolonged period of synaptic integration (Toni and Schinder, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Toni and Schinder, 2015).

claim: Newborn GC differentiation is followed by a prolonged period of synaptic integration.
source: Adult neurogenesis proceeds in a step-wise manner, with activated stem cells producing rapidly dividing progenitor cells that exit cell cycle and differentiate into newborn GCs or undergo programmed cell death, followed by a prolonged period of synaptic integration (Toni and Schinder, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Toni and Schinder, 2015).

claim: Stem cell quiescence, progenitor proliferation, survival and maturation are activity-dependent processes.
source: Stem cell quiescence, progenitor proliferation, survival and maturation are activity-dependent processes that enable neural network activity to influence the development of new circuitry.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about adult neurogenesis.

claim: Activity-dependent processes enable neural network activity to influence the development of new circuitry.
source: Stem cell quiescence, progenitor proliferation, survival and maturation are activity-dependent processes that enable neural network activity to influence the development of new circuitry.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the functional significance of activity-dependent neurogenesis.

claim: GABA receptor-mediated mechanisms underlie many aspects of activity-dependent regulation in adult neurogenesis.
source: It is well established that GABA receptor-mediated mechanisms underlie many aspects of activity-dependent regulation, largely via GABAA receptor-mediated depolarization of proliferating progenitors and newborn neurons (Tozuka et al., 2005; Ge et al., 2006; Jagasia et al., 2009; Dieni et al., 2012; Chancey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: GABAA receptor-mediated depolarization of proliferating progenitors and newborn neurons underlies activity-dependent regulation.
source: It is well established that GABA receptor-mediated mechanisms underlie many aspects of activity-dependent regulation, largely via GABAA receptor-mediated depolarization of proliferating progenitors and newborn neurons (Tozuka et al., 2005; Ge et al., 2006; Jagasia et al., 2009; Dieni et al., 2012; Chancey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Optogenetic manipulation of PVs alters stem cell quiescence and progenitor proliferation.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVs) are particularly important mediators of activity-dependent regulation, since optogenetic manipulation of PVs alters stem cell quiescence and progenitor proliferation, as well as newborn GC survival and maturation (Song et al., 2012; Song et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Song et al., 2012; Song et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016).

claim: Optogenetic manipulation of PVs alters newborn GC survival and maturation.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVs) are particularly important mediators of activity-dependent regulation, since optogenetic manipulation of PVs alters stem cell quiescence and progenitor proliferation, as well as newborn GC survival and maturation (Song et al., 2012; Song et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Song et al., 2012; Song et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016).

claim: PVs comprise just 10–20% of dentate GABAergic interneurons.
source: PVs comprise just 10–20% of dentate GABAergic interneurons but have extensive axonal arbors that form powerful perisomatic synapses comprised of many release sites (Kraushaar and Jonas, 2000; Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kraushaar and Jonas, 2000; Hu et al., 2014).

claim: PVs have extensive axonal arbors that form powerful perisomatic synapses comprised of many release sites.
source: PVs comprise just 10–20% of dentate GABAergic interneurons but have extensive axonal arbors that form powerful perisomatic synapses comprised of many release sites (Kraushaar and Jonas, 2000; Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kraushaar and Jonas, 2000; Hu et al., 2014).

claim: At individual PV release sites, the cleft [GABA] is high and brief.
source: At individual release sites, the cleft [GABA] is high and brief such that receptor kinetics primarily determine the time course of miniature GABAA-receptor mediated postsynaptic currents (GPSCs) (Overstreet et al., 2002; Mozrzymas, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Overstreet et al., 2002; Mozrzymas, 2004).

claim: Receptor kinetics primarily determine the time course of miniature GPSCs at individual PV release sites.
source: At individual release sites, the cleft [GABA] is high and brief such that receptor kinetics primarily determine the time course of miniature GABAA-receptor mediated postsynaptic currents (GPSCs) (Overstreet et al., 2002; Mozrzymas, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Overstreet et al., 2002; Mozrzymas, 2004).

claim: Synchronous vesicle release across multiple active sites in combination with rapid diffusion of GABA generates large unitary GPSCs with fast rise and decay kinetics.
source: Synchronous vesicle release across multiple active sites in combination with rapid diffusion of GABA away from spatially-segregated sites generates large unitary GPSCs with hallmark fast rise and decay kinetics (Bartos et al., 2002; Overstreet and Westbrook, 2003; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Strüber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Bartos et al., 2002; Overstreet and Westbrook, 2003; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Strüber et al., 2015).

claim: Fast IPSCs allow PVs to precisely control the time window of spike initiation and synchrony of downstream targets.
source: Together with intrinsic features that enable PVs to rapidly translate synaptic excitation into action potential firing, fast IPSCs allow PVs to precisely control the time window of spike initiation and synchrony of downstream targets (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Hu et al., 2014; Strüber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Hu et al., 2014; Strüber et al., 2015).

claim: PVs exhibit enriched connectivity motifs supporting lateral inhibition between GCs in the dentate gyrus.
source: In the dentate gyrus, PVs exhibit enriched connectivity motifs supporting lateral inhibition between GCs (Espinoza et al., 2018), but a relative lack of fast inhibition contributes to enhanced synaptic activation of immature GCs compared to mature GCs (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Espinoza et al., 2018).

claim: A relative lack of fast inhibition contributes to enhanced synaptic activation of immature GCs compared to mature GCs.
source: In the dentate gyrus, PVs exhibit enriched connectivity motifs supporting lateral inhibition between GCs (Espinoza et al., 2018), but a relative lack of fast inhibition contributes to enhanced synaptic activation of immature GCs compared to mature GCs (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013).

claim: Young adult-born GCs exclusively exhibit small GPSCs with slow rise times and decay phases.
source: In contrast to mature GCs, young adult-born GCs exclusively exhibit small GPSCs with slow rise times and decay phases (Espósito et al., 2005; Overstreet Wadiche et al., 2005; Markwardt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Espósito et al., 2005; Overstreet Wadiche et al., 2005; Markwardt et al., 2009).

claim: Electrical and PV-evoked GPSCs with fast rise times do not appear until adult-born neurons are about 1 month postmitotic.
source: Electrical and PV-evoked GPSCs with fast rise times do not appear until adult-born neurons are about 1 month postmitotic (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016; Groisman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016; Groisman et al., 2020).

claim: Small GPSC amplitudes in newborn GCs are readily explained by few release sites across the small somato-dendritic domain of developing GCs.
source: While small GPSC amplitudes are readily explained by few release sites across the small somato-dendritic domain of developing GCs, the slow kinetics are more difficult to understand.
evidence: This is inferred from established knowledge about synaptic transmission and neuronal development.

claim: Triple-transgenic mice expressing Pomc-EGFP, PvalbCre-driven ChR2 (H134R)-EYFP were generated to examine GABAergic signaling from PVs in the DG.
source: To examine GABAergic signaling from PVs in the DG, we generated triple-transgenic mice expressing Pomc-EGFP to identify newborn GCs, along with PvalbCre-driven ChR2 (H134R)-EYFP to optogenetically activate PVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Light pulses between 0.1 and 1 ms reliably triggered action potentials in PVs with correlated GPSCs in mature GCs.
source: In the presence of NBQX and CPP, we measured reliable action potentials in PVs with correlated GPSCs in mature GCs using light pulses between 0.1 and 1 ms (470 nm, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Light pulses longer than 0.5 ms typically triggered two action potentials in PVs.
source: Light pulses longer than 0.5 ms typically triggered two action potentials in PVs, which in turn triggered a 2nd small peak on the decay phase of the initial GPSC, likely resulting from strong paired-pulse depression of GABA release from the same axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Two action potentials in PVs triggered a 2nd small peak on the decay phase of the initial GPSC, likely resulting from strong paired-pulse depression of GABA release.
source: Light pulses longer than 0.5 ms typically triggered two action potentials in PVs, which in turn triggered a 2nd small peak on the decay phase of the initial GPSC, likely resulting from strong paired-pulse depression of GABA release from the same axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: PV spikes reliably followed trains of light pulses at 100 Hz with at least one spike.
source: Cell-attached recordings revealed PV spikes reliably followed trains of light pulses at 100 Hz with at least one spike (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Light-evoked GPSCs in mature GCs were blocked by TTX.
source: Light-evoked GPSCs in mature GCs were blocked by TTX (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or gabazine (n = 7, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 1A.

claim: Light-evoked GPSCs in mature GCs were blocked by gabazine.
source: Light-evoked GPSCs in mature GCs were blocked by TTX (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or gabazine (n = 7, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Optogenetic activation provides sufficient depolarization for action potential-dependent GABAergic synaptic transmission from PVs.
source: Together these results demonstrate optogenetic activation provides sufficient depolarization for action potential-dependent GABAergic synaptic transmission from PVs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing TTX-sensitive light-evoked GPSCs.

claim: Low frequency stimulation (0.1 Hz) using 1 ms light pulses generated large GPSCs in mature GCs and small but reliable GPSCs in newborn GCs.
source: Low frequency stimulation (0.1 Hz) using 1 ms light pulses generated large GPSCs in mature GCs and small but reliable GPSCs in newborn GCs, with both displaying paired-pulse depression (PPD; 200 ms ISI; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both mature and newborn GCs displayed paired-pulse depression in response to PV stimulation.
source: Low frequency stimulation (0.1 Hz) using 1 ms light pulses generated large GPSCs in mature GCs and small but reliable GPSCs in newborn GCs, with both displaying paired-pulse depression (PPD; 200 ms ISI; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was a greater than 10-fold difference in GPSC amplitude between mature and newborn GCs (1855 ± 312 pA in mature compared to 110 ± 25 pA in newborn GCs; n = 11).
source: Despite a greater than 10-fold difference in GPSC amplitude (1855 ± 312 pA in mature compared to 110 ± 25 pA in newborn GCs; n = 11), there was a positive correlation between the GPSC amplitude across pairs suggesting the amplitude was dependent on the number of activated PVs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the GPSC amplitude across pairs of mature and newborn GCs.
source: Despite a greater than 10-fold difference in GPSC amplitude (1855 ± 312 pA in mature compared to 110 ± 25 pA in newborn GCs; n = 11), there was a positive correlation between the GPSC amplitude across pairs suggesting the amplitude was dependent on the number of activated PVs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The positive correlation between GPSC amplitudes suggests the amplitude was dependent on the number of activated PVs.
source: Despite a greater than 10-fold difference in GPSC amplitude (1855 ± 312 pA in mature compared to 110 ± 25 pA in newborn GCs; n = 11), there was a positive correlation between the GPSC amplitude across pairs suggesting the amplitude was dependent on the number of activated PVs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed correlation in the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PV-evoked GPSCs in mature GCs had sub-millisecond rise-times.
source: Normalizing mature and newborn GPSCs to the peak amplitude revealed highly contrasting kinetics. Whereas PV-evoked GPSCs in mature GCs had sub-millisecond rise-times, GPSCs in newborn GCs had slower rise and decay times, and stronger PPD (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GPSCs in newborn GCs had slower rise and decay times compared to mature GCs.
source: Normalizing mature and newborn GPSCs to the peak amplitude revealed highly contrasting kinetics. Whereas PV-evoked GPSCs in mature GCs had sub-millisecond rise-times, GPSCs in newborn GCs had slower rise and decay times, and stronger PPD (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GPSCs in newborn GCs had stronger paired-pulse depression compared to mature GCs.
source: Normalizing mature and newborn GPSCs to the peak amplitude revealed highly contrasting kinetics. Whereas PV-evoked GPSCs in mature GCs had sub-millisecond rise-times, GPSCs in newborn GCs had slower rise and decay times, and stronger PPD (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no correlation between GPSC amplitude and rise or decay times across cell pairs.
source: There was no correlation between GPSC amplitude and rise or decay times across cell pairs, suggesting that distinct response kinetics were independent of the number of stimulated PVs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Distinct response kinetics were independent of the number of stimulated PVs.
source: There was no correlation between GPSC amplitude and rise or decay times across cell pairs, suggesting that distinct response kinetics were independent of the number of stimulated PVs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The kinetic differences between newborn and mature GPSCs persisted at sub-millisecond light intensities.
source: Light pulses < 1 ms generated very small or absent GPSCs in newborn GCs and sometimes failures in mature GCs, but the kinetic differences between newborn and mature GPSCs persisted (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PVs generate GPSCs in mature GCs with the expected fast kinetics of synapses from PV-expressing fast-spiking basket cells.
source: Together these results show that PVs generate GPSCs in mature GCs with the expected fast kinetics of synapses from PV-expressing fast-spiking basket cells (Bartos et al., 2002), but that newborn GCs have slower GPSCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and supported by citation to prior work (Bartos et al., 2002).

claim: Newborn GCs lack α1 subunits that are associated with rapid channel gating and fast decay kinetics.
source: The slow GPSCs in newborn GCs could result from the expression of distinct GABAA receptors, since newborn GCs lack α1 subunits that are associated with rapid channel gating and fast decay kinetics (Overstreet Wadiche et al., 2005; Karten et al., 2006; Picton and Fisher, 2007; Eyre et al., 2012; Dixon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Overstreet Wadiche et al., 2005; Karten et al., 2006; Picton and Fisher, 2007; Eyre et al., 2012; Dixon et al., 2014).

claim: α1 subunits are associated with rapid channel gating and fast decay kinetics.
source: The slow GPSCs in newborn GCs could result from the expression of distinct GABAA receptors, since newborn GCs lack α1 subunits that are associated with rapid channel gating and fast decay kinetics (Overstreet Wadiche et al., 2005; Karten et al., 2006; Picton and Fisher, 2007; Eyre et al., 2012; Dixon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Overstreet Wadiche et al., 2005; Karten et al., 2006; Picton and Fisher, 2007; Eyre et al., 2012; Dixon et al., 2014).

claim: A knockin mouse with a photoswitchable α1 GABAA receptor subunit replaces its wild-type counterpart, allowing selective light-induced antagonism of α1-containing receptors.
source: In this approach, a knockin mouse with a photoswitchable α1 GABAA receptor subunit replaces its wild-type counterpart, allowing selective light-induced antagonism of α1-containing receptors (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Lin et al., 2015) describing the LiGABAR mouse line.

claim: In darkness, the tethered antagonist (PAG1C) blocks α1 containing receptors in LiGABAR mice.
source: In darkness, the tethered antagonist (PAG1C) blocks α1 containing receptors, and preconditioning with 390 nm light alleviates antagonism whereas 480 nm light reinstates it.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the LiGABAR system from prior work.

claim: Preconditioning with 390 nm light alleviates antagonism of α1 containing receptors in LiGABAR mice.
source: In darkness, the tethered antagonist (PAG1C) blocks α1 containing receptors, and preconditioning with 390 nm light alleviates antagonism whereas 480 nm light reinstates it.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the LiGABAR system from prior work.

claim: 480 nm light reinstates antagonism of α1 containing receptors in LiGABAR mice.
source: In darkness, the tethered antagonist (PAG1C) blocks α1 containing receptors, and preconditioning with 390 nm light alleviates antagonism whereas 480 nm light reinstates it.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the LiGABAR system from prior work.

claim: IML stimulation generated GPSCs with relatively slow rise and decay phases that were minimally blocked by light inactivation of α1 subunits in mature GCs.
source: In mature GCs, IML stimulation generated GPSCs with relatively slow rise and decay phases that were minimally blocked by light inactivation of α1 subunits whereas GCL stimulation evoked GPSC with faster rise and decay phases that were blocked to a greater extent by light (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: GCL stimulation evoked GPSCs with faster rise and decay phases that were blocked to a greater extent by light inactivation of α1 subunits in mature GCs.
source: In mature GCs, IML stimulation generated GPSCs with relatively slow rise and decay phases that were minimally blocked by light inactivation of α1 subunits whereas GCL stimulation evoked GPSC with faster rise and decay phases that were blocked to a greater extent by light (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Fast GPSCs arise at perisomatic synapses with high α1 content.
source: This supports the idea that fast GPSCs arise at perisomatic synapses with high α1 content, and indeed there was a correlation between the rise time of GPSCs and the percentage of photosensitive current (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was a correlation between the rise time of GPSCs and the percentage of photosensitive current.
source: This supports the idea that fast GPSCs arise at perisomatic synapses with high α1 content, and indeed there was a correlation between the rise time of GPSCs and the percentage of photosensitive current (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Antagonizing GABAA receptors containing α1 subunits does not alter kinetics of GPSCs evoked by electrical stimulation of many synapses.
source: However, the time courses of fast and slow GPSCs were not altered (Figure 2D), illustrating that antagonizing GABAA receptors containing α1 subunits does not alter kinetics of GPSCs evoked by electrical stimulation of many synapses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Subunit-specific receptor gating dominates the time course at individual synapses.
source: While subunit composition is the main factor determining the the decay phase of synaptic currents at an individual synapse (i.e. mIPSCs Eyre et al., 2012), additional factors come into play when tens to hundreds of release sites are activated together.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Eyre et al., 2012).

claim: Additional factors beyond subunit composition contribute to GPSC kinetics when tens to hundreds of release sites are activated together.
source: While subunit composition is the main factor determining the the decay phase of synaptic currents at an individual synapse (i.e. mIPSCs Eyre et al., 2012), additional factors come into play when tens to hundreds of release sites are activated together.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by citation.

claim: GAD67-GFP reporter mice identify adult-born GCs that are ~2–4 weeks postmitotic.
source: We then crossed α1 LiGABAR mice with GAD67-GFP reporter mice that identify adult-born GCs that are ~2–4 weeks postmitotic, thus slightly 'older' than Pomc-EGPF newborn GCs (Cabezas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Cabezas et al., 2013).

claim: GAD67-GFP labeled GCs are slightly 'older' than Pomc-EGFP newborn GCs.
source: We then crossed α1 LiGABAR mice with GAD67-GFP reporter mice that identify adult-born GCs that are ~2–4 weeks postmitotic, thus slightly 'older' than Pomc-EGPF newborn GCs (Cabezas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression patterns of the two reporter lines.

claim: Blocking α1 receptors with light had a smaller effect on the amplitude of GPSCs in young GCs than in mature GCs.
source: Blocking α1 receptors with light had a smaller effect on the amplitude of GPSCs in young GCs than in mature GCs, with a measurable effect suggesting low levels of functional α1 expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Young GCs have low levels of functional α1 expression.
source: Blocking α1 receptors with light had a smaller effect on the amplitude of GPSCs in young GCs than in mature GCs, with a measurable effect suggesting low levels of functional α1 expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Light-induced block of α1 subunits did not affect GPSC kinetics in either mature or immature GCs.
source: Light-induced block of α1 subunits did not affect GPSC kinetics in either mature or immature GCs, noting again that the GPSCs in young GCs had slower rise times and decay phases compared to neighboring mature GCs (Figure 2G; rise time: 4.0 ± 0.4 ms vs. 1.2 ± 0.2 ms, p<0.0001; decay: 55.2 ± 3.7 ms vs. 26.2 ± 3.2 ms, p<0.0001, paired t-tests, n = 12 each).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: GPSCs in young GCs had slower rise times (4.0 ± 0.4 ms) compared to neighboring mature GCs (1.2 ± 0.2 ms).
source: Light-induced block of α1 subunits did not affect GPSC kinetics in either mature or immature GCs, noting again that the GPSCs in young GCs had slower rise times and decay phases compared to neighboring mature GCs (Figure 2G; rise time: 4.0 ± 0.4 ms vs. 1.2 ± 0.2 ms, p<0.0001; decay: 55.2 ± 3.7 ms vs. 26.2 ± 3.2 ms, p<0.0001, paired t-tests, n = 12 each).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: GPSCs in young GCs had slower decay phases (55.2 ± 3.7 ms) compared to neighboring mature GCs (26.2 ± 3.2 ms).
source: Light-induced block of α1 subunits did not affect GPSC kinetics in either mature or immature GCs, noting again that the GPSCs in young GCs had slower rise times and decay phases compared to neighboring mature GCs (Figure 2G; rise time: 4.0 ± 0.4 ms vs. 1.2 ± 0.2 ms, p<0.0001; decay: 55.2 ± 3.7 ms vs. 26.2 ± 3.2 ms, p<0.0001, paired t-tests, n = 12 each).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: α1-mediated GPSCs in young GCs had both slower rise times and decay times than in neighboring mature GCs.
source: However, we observed that α1-mediated GPSCs in young GCs had both slower rise times and decay times than in neighboring mature GCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immature GCs express lower levels of α1-containing receptors.
source: Together these results confirm that immature GCs express lower levels of α1-containing receptors, but indicate this differential expression pattern cannot explain the slow GPSC kinetics.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on α1 photoinhibition.

claim: Differential α1 expression cannot explain the slow GPSC kinetics in immature GCs.
source: Together these results confirm that immature GCs express lower levels of α1-containing receptors, but indicate this differential expression pattern cannot explain the slow GPSC kinetics.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that α1-mediated GPSCs still have slow kinetics in young GCs.

claim: Electrical stimulation generates slow GPSCs in newborn GCs with characteristics similar to volume transmission from neurogliaform interneurons.
source: In fact, electrical stimulation generates slow GPSCs in newborn GCs with characteristics that are similar to volume transmission from neurogliaform interneurons wherein the spatial-temporal [GABA] profile dictates the slow GPSC properties rather than subunit composition (Szabadics et al., 2007; Markwardt et al., 2009; Karayannis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Szabadics et al., 2007; Markwardt et al., 2009; Karayannis et al., 2010).

claim: In volume transmission from neurogliaform interneurons, the spatial-temporal [GABA] profile dictates the slow GPSC properties rather than subunit composition.
source: In fact, electrical stimulation generates slow GPSCs in newborn GCs with characteristics that are similar to volume transmission from neurogliaform interneurons wherein the spatial-temporal [GABA] profile dictates the slow GPSC properties rather than subunit composition (Szabadics et al., 2007; Markwardt et al., 2009; Karayannis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Szabadics et al., 2007; Markwardt et al., 2009; Karayannis et al., 2010).

claim: High-affinity antagonists are expected to reduce synaptic currents to a similar extent regardless of the synaptic [GABA].

evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and supported by citations (Overstreet and Westbrook, 2003; Biró and Nusser, 2005).

claim: The peak of the PV-GPSC reversed near the calculated ECl- whereas the nNOS-GPSC reversed at a more hyperpolarized potential.
source: The peak of the PV-GPSC reversed near the calculated ECl- whereas the nNOS-GPSC reversed at a more hyperpolarized potential, as expected for somatic and dendritic localized synapses, respectively (Groisman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation (Groisman et al., 2020).

claim: The slow component of the PV-GPSC (measured 50 ms after the stimulus) had a similar reversal potential as the peak, consistent with a somatic localization.
source: Importantly, the slow component of the PV-GPSC (measured 50 ms after the stimulus) had a similar reversal potential as the peak, consistent with a somatic localization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both reducing the duration of the light pulse or using the precondition stimulus to reduce the density of active sites speeded the GPSC decay phase in mature GCs.
source: Both reducing the duration of the light pulse or using the precondition stimulus to reduce the density of active sites speeded the GPSC decay phase in mature GCs, consistent with spillover contributing the slow decay phase (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The reduction of GABA release during paired-pulse stimuli generated a detectable speeding of 2nd GPSC in both mature GCs (half-width reduced to 8.9 ± 0.6 ms from 11.8 ± 1.0 ms) and newborn GCs (reduced to 31.4 ± 1.8 ms from 41.9 ± 1.7 ms).
source: Even the reduction of GABA release during paired-pulse stimuli generated a detectable speeding of 2nd GPSC in both mature GCs (half-width reduced to 8.9 ± 0.6 ms from 11.8 ± 1.0 ms, n = 30, p<0.001 paired t-test) and newborn GCs (reduced to 31.4 ± 1.8 ms from 41.9 ± 1.7 ms, n = 21, p<0.001 paired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data.

claim: Prolongation of the mature GPSC decay phase by NO711 depended on the density of active release sites.
source: Prolongation of the mature GPSC decay phase by NO711 also depended on the density of active release sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reducing the light intensity initially produced smaller GPSCs with variable latencies and very fast rise times in mature GCs, presumably reflecting GABA release from single axons with different thresholds of activation.
source: In an example of a simultaneous recording from a mature and newborn GC, reducing the light intensity initially produced smaller GPSCs with variable latencies and very fast rise times in mature GCs, presumably reflecting GABA release from single axons with different thresholds of activation (Figure 7A, blue symbols and traces).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At lowest light intensities, fast GPSCs often failed but close inspection of the apparent failures revealed both failure or small GPSCs with slow rise times.
source: At lowest light intensities, fast GPSCs often failed but close inspection of the apparent failures (red traces) revealed both failure or small GPSCs with slow rise times (Figure 7A right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Averaging 'successes' in mature GCs when fast GPSCs failed revealed a slow GPSC.
source: Averaging 'successes' in mature GCs when fast GPSCs failed revealed a slow GPSC (black trace, Figure 7B), that was larger than the correlated averaged GPSC in the newborn GC, perhaps due to the high number of failures (green trace; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Slow GPSCs in the mature and newborn GC had similar amplitudes and rise times that were dramatically different from fast GPSCs.
source: Comparing only successes revealed that slow GPSCs in the mature (black) and newborn (green) GC had similar amplitudes and rise times that were dramatically different from fast GPSCs (blue; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The decay time course of the slow GPSC in mature GCs was slightly faster than the decay phase of GPSCs in newborn GCs.
source: The decay time course of the slow GPSC in mature GCs was slightly faster than the decay phase of GPSCs in newborn GCs (normalized traces, Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The isolated slow GPSC in mature GCs scaled to the slow decay phase of the fast GPSC.
source: The isolated slow GPSC in mature GCs also scaled to the slow decay phase of the fast GPSC (dotted line, Figure 7B right), suggesting that this spillover component accounts for the slow decay phase in fast GPSCs that is enhanced by NO711 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and inferred from comparison with Figure 3B.

claim: Isolated slow GPSCs were found in 7/12 mature GCs with an amplitude of 19 ± 2 pA and rise times of 2.9 ± 0.5 ms.
source: By sorting traces in mature GCs at just-threshold light intensities for generating fast GPSCs (see methods), we found isolated slow GPSCs in 7/12 mature GCs with an amplitude of 19 ± 2 pA and rise times of 2.9 ± 0.5 ms (n = 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data.

claim: NO711 (2 µM) increased the amplitude and rise time of slow GPSCs in mature GCs.
source: Consistent with spillover signaling, NO711 (2 µM) increased the amplitude and rise time of these slow GPSCs (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In mature GCs that did not exhibit slow GPSCs at sub-threshold light intensities, NO711 had no effect on the fast GPSCs generated at threshold light intensities.
source: In contrast, in mature GCs that did not exhibit slow GPSCs at sub-threshold light intensities, NO711 had no effect on the fast GPSCs generated at threshold light intensities (Figure 7D, n = 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Independent synaptic and spillover GPSCs in mature GCs are similar to fast and slow GPSCs in cerebellar GCs that arise from directly-connected and remote terminals, respectively.
source: Thus, these independent synaptic and spillover GPSCs in mature GCs are similar to fast and slow GPSCs in cerebellar GCs that arise from directly-connected and remote terminals, respectively (Rossi and Hamann, 1998).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation (Rossi and Hamann, 1998).

claim: PVs can signal to both mature and newborn GCs via spillover transmission.
source: These results suggest that PVs can signal to both mature and newborn GCs via spillover transmission, whereas only mature GCs exhibit direct synaptic connections.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing slow GPSCs in both cell types.

claim: Only mature GCs exhibit direct synaptic connections from PVs.
source: These results suggest that PVs can signal to both mature and newborn GCs via spillover transmission, whereas only mature GCs exhibit direct synaptic connections.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing fast GPSCs only in mature GCs.

claim: Slow GPSCs regulate activity-dependent maturation and survival of newborn GCs via depolarization.
source: Slow GPSCs regulate activity-dependent maturation and survival of newborn GCs via depolarization (Ge et al., 2006; Jagasia et al., 2009; Song et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Ge et al., 2006; Jagasia et al., 2009; Song et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016).

claim: Slow GPSCs are first detected in a minority of GC progenitors.
source: Slow GPSCs are first detected in a minority of GC progenitors (Wang et al., 2005), arising from PV but not somatostatin or vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Wang et al., 2005; Song et al., 2013).

claim: Slow GPSCs arise from PV but not somatostatin or vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons.
source: Slow GPSCs are first detected in a minority of GC progenitors (Wang et al., 2005), arising from PV but not somatostatin or vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Song et al., 2013).

claim: Pomc-EGFP identifies an early postmitotic neuronal stage when essentially all newborn GCs exhibit slow GPSCs and first acquire functional excitatory synapses from hilar mossy cells.
source: Pomc-EGFP identifies an early postmitotic neuronal stage when essentially all newborn GCs exhibit slow GPSCs and first acquire functional excitatory synapses from hilar mossy cells (Overstreet et al., 2004; Chancey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Overstreet et al., 2004; Chancey et al., 2014).

claim: GABAergic depolarization allows voltage-dependent unblock of NMDARs that is required for activity-dependent incorporation of AMPARs at functionally silent NMDAR-only synapses.
source: GABAergic depolarization allows voltage-dependent unblock of NMDARs that is required for activity-dependent incorporation of AMPARs at functionally silent NMDAR-only synapses (Chancey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chancey et al., 2013).

claim: Both glutamatergic mossy cells and mature GCs recruit disynaptic GABA release to newborn GCs.
source: Both glutamatergic mossy cells and mature GCs recruit disynaptic GABA release to newborn GCs, with the slow time course of the GABAergic conductance matching the time course of the NMDAR-EPSC, suggesting circuitry for coupling GABA and glutamate signaling that together allow rapid synaptic integration of newborn GCs in response to network activity (Chancey et al., 2014; Alvarez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Chancey et al., 2014; Alvarez et al., 2016).

claim: The slow time course of the GABAergic conductance matches the time course of the NMDAR-EPSC.
source: Both glutamatergic mossy cells and mature GCs recruit disynaptic GABA release to newborn GCs, with the slow time course of the GABAergic conductance matching the time course of the NMDAR-EPSC, suggesting circuitry for coupling GABA and glutamate signaling that together allow rapid synaptic integration of newborn GCs in response to network activity (Chancey et al., 2014; Alvarez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Chancey et al., 2014; Alvarez et al., 2016).

claim: Fast GPSCs from PV and SST interneurons do not appear in adult-born GCs until >4 weeks post-mitosis.
source: Interestingly, fast GPSCs from PV and SST interneurons do not appear in adult-born GCs until >4 weeks post-mitosis, when dendrites have extended through the molecular layer and perforant path excitatory synapses are established (Espósito et al., 2005; Mongiat et al., 2009; Dieni et al., 2013; Groisman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Espósito et al., 2005; Mongiat et al., 2009; Dieni et al., 2013; Groisman et al., 2020).

claim: The dependence on non-canonical mechanisms of GABAergic synaptic depolarization at early stages suggests that newborn GCs might lack the molecular machinery for conventional GABAergic synapse formation.
source: The dependence on non-canonical mechanisms of GABAergic synaptic depolarization at early stages suggests that newborn GCs might lack the molecular machinery for conventional GABAergic synapse formation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental observations.

claim: The duration and amplitude of unitary GPSCs differs with distance between individual PVs and postsynaptic GCs.
source: Interestingly, the duration and amplitude of unitary GPSCs differs with distance between individual PVs and postsynaptic GCs, and these differences may confer non-uniformity that enables emergence of functionally independent focal gamma bursts (Strüber et al., 2015; Strüber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Strüber et al., 2015; Strüber et al., 2017).

claim: Differences in unitary GPSC properties may confer non-uniformity that enables emergence of functionally independent focal gamma bursts.
source: Interestingly, the duration and amplitude of unitary GPSCs differs with distance between individual PVs and postsynaptic GCs, and these differences may confer non-uniformity that enables emergence of functionally independent focal gamma bursts (Strüber et al., 2015; Strüber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculated based on prior work (Strüber et al., 2015; Strüber et al., 2017).

claim: It is plausible that slow spillover from PVs, dependent on the density of active terminals, can contribute to non-uniformity of GABAA conductances to support focal gamma frequency oscillations.
source: Thus, it is plausible that slow spillover from PVs, dependent on the density of active terminals, can also contribute to non-uniformity of GABAA conductances to support focal gamma frequency oscillations.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental findings and prior knowledge.
